# Notify Me About This Session, Not All Sessions ​

October 18, 2026 · Michael Richman

## Manage alert overload ​

I don't want to get live alerts from all sessions. But for one or two, ping me as soon as you're ready!

On a busy day I may have a dozen or more coding agent sessions going.

I don't want to get live alerts from most of them – they'll finish when they finish, and I'll look when I look.

But one or two I'm actively thinking about and iterating on – the ones where I want to know when a turn is done or the agent needs an answer from me.

The problem with most coding agent mobile apps is app-wide notifications .

Their notification settings are a single boolean – Notifications ON or Notifications OFF.

Leave it on and, after a day of alerts from every coding and chat session, you stop looking. Turn it off and you miss the ones you're tracking.

## Pick the sessions that get your attention ​

With Cmd+Ctrl, push notifications work on a session-by-session basis. Tap the bell on a session – Get notifications – and that session pushes to your phone when the agent finishes. Every other session stays quiet.

## On my radar, still important but without the ping ​

There's a middle tier between "notify me" and "ignore it" because some sessions I still want on my radar even if I don't want push notifications. Hence, Cmd+Ctrl On my radar .

An "On my radar" session sits at the top of your list where you can glance at it, but it never notifies. It's for the session I want to keep an eye on without being interrupted by it – a long-running job on the back burner that I don't want to forget.

Notify me, keep it on my radar, or leave it alone until I go looking.

So a typical day looks like this: one or two sessions with notifications on, a handful on my radar, and everything else out of the way until I go looking.

## What the other apps do ​

None of the main coding agents' native mobile apps do this. It's all or nothing when it comes to alerts.

- Claude Code Remote Control has two account-wide push toggles – one for when Claude decides to notify you, one for when it needs input. The docs say there's no finer control. The Claude desktop app can mute notifications for a whole project.

- OpenAI Codex has global notification settings in the ChatGPT apps. Per-thread muting is an open feature request .

- GitHub Copilot in GitHub Mobile shows live progress notifications for agent sessions, switched off globally in Settings. Its push categories have no agent category, and its docs show no per-session control.

It's very useful to be able to say "alert on this session, not those".

This may seem like a small feature on paper. In practice it's what makes running many agents from a phone workable – your attention goes to the sessions you've decided matter, and nothing else nags you.

# Refute, Don't Review ​

October 11, 2026 · Michael Richman

Assume this is broken and prove it. If you can't, we're good.

## Refute vs. Review: What's the difference? ​

We all know a coding agent's first pass is flawed. The question is, how do you uncover the flaws? Today's typical answer is AI code review – and whole companies are built on that.

I've actually had far more success with Refute than Review .

The problems with agent review and especially agent self-review are well known. Moving review out of the main context has helped, but most review agents still start by assuming the code is correct.

Tell an agent that the code is broken, and it will go looking for the problems it assumes exist. That's good.

By contrast, tell an agent that the code is broken and to prove it, and it will go looking for the problems it assumes exist. If it comes up empty-handed, you're far more likely to have clean code than with code review alone.

Anecdotally, on anything but the simplest change, I have never had the first refuter come back empty-handed. That's frightening for what was getting through before, and reassuring for what it catches now.

## Power in the loop ​

An adversarial stance for review isn't new of course. Where refutation really pays off is when you run it in a loop .

When the refutation agent finds issues, I have my main agent fix them and then repeat the refutation until it converges towards full resolution.

## Human attention is the scarce resource ​

By the time an agent tells me something is ready for review, it should have survived several rounds of trying to break it. All I want then is a short list of what only a human can check.

None of this replaces architectural review and it doesn't fully replace code review. But refutation comes first and gets the higher priority in my workflow.

## The Refutation prompt ​

The core of the prompt is simple:

> Your job is to REFUTE a change, not review it. Default to: this is broken, and prove it. A finding counts only with evidence: a failing test, or a command plus its output, or a line-numbered path from input to wrong result. "Could not break it" is valid if you list what you tried.

A finding counts only with evidence: a failing test, or a command plus its output, or a line-numbered path from input to wrong result. "Could not break it" is valid if you list what you tried.

That guidance is accompanied by the requirement, the commit range, the test command, and a few angles to attack. Here's the full prompt template and here's an example from real life .

Two things matter most:

- A fresh sub-agent. The refuter gets the brief -- requirement, commit range, test command -- and not the author's reasoning. If the sub-agent shares the author's context, it shares the author's blind spots.

- Evidence or it doesn't count. A finding without a failing test or a repro gets dropped. That kills the plausible-sounding false positives.

## Loop and converge ​

- Fix every confirmed defect. Keep the refuter's failing test.

- Dispatch a new refuter with the same prompt and the new commit range.

- Stop when a round confirms nothing, or only minor defects outside the requirement.

- Escalate to me when it stops converging: a round finds as many defects as the last, or worse ones; the same invariant breaks again in a new form; or five rounds have passed.

When the refutation rounds don't converge, the problem usually isn't the code; it's the design. That's when I step in.

I've packaged the prompt and the loop as an agent skill you can install in Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI and others: cmdctrlai/refute .

I hope you find this useful. I sure have.
